items.title: [mail-parser] mail-parser: One hostile attachment aborts `write_attachments()` and silently drops the rest of the batch
items.summary:
Impactwrite_attachments() called _safe_attachment_filename() and write_sample() inside its loopwith no guard, so a single crafted attachment raised out of the whole save. Every attachmentafter the malicious one was silently never written, with no error surfaced to a caller thatcatches only MailParserError.That is an evasion primitive as much as an availability bug: a sender puts one poisoned partfirst and the real payload second, and the payload never reaches the extraction directory thata downstream scanner or sandbox reads — while it still reaches the recipient's mail clientintact. The tool's output diverges from the bytes actually in the message, which is the samefailure mode as the filename-sanitizing bypass inGHSA-fr3h-cpq2-9496.Three shapes were reachable, all from attacker-controlled MIME metadata:NUL smuggled through RFC 2231 — filename*=us-ascii''evil%00.bin decodes to a NUL in thefilename during parsing and raised ValueError out of the name check;overlong basename — a filename longer than NAME_MAX (e.g. 300 characters) raisedOSError: File name too long from open(), after creating a zero-byte stub on disk;undecodable payload — a body that is not valid base64 raised binascii.Error (aValueError subclass) from the decode performed inside the open() block.import tempfile, mailparserraw = ("Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary=b

"       "--b
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
"       "Content-Disposition: attachment; filename*=us-ascii''evil%00.bin

xx
"       "--b
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
"       "Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=good.bin

yy
"       "--b--
")mp = mailparser.parse_from_string(raw)     # parse itself is fine; safe_filename is Nonemp.write_attachments(tempfile.mkdtemp())# 4.6.0 - 4.6.2 -> ValueError, and good.bin is never written# 4.6.3         -> logs "Skipped attachment with invalid filename: 'evil\x00.bin'";#                  good.bin is writtenparse() itself was never affected — it catches the ValueError — so only the write path wasunguarded. The reject-paths that made this reachable were introduced with the filenamesanitizing in 4.6.0 (PR #165).PatchesFixed in 4.6.3. write_attachments() now logs and skips a single unusable attachmentinstead of aborting the batch:an invalid filename is caught and skipped;overlong basenames are truncated to 240 UTF-8 bytes, preserving the extension, rather thanreaching open();the base64 decode moved before open(), so a failure leaves no zero-byte stub, and it nowrepairs padding and alphabet errors the way mail clients do (matching MIME::Base64 on 2008cases) — rejecting them let a sender append one character to make an attachment vanish fromthe extraction directory while it still reached the recipient;MailParserPathError is deliberately not caught by the per-attachment handler: acontainment failure is not a per-attachment problem, and path-containment checks now raiseMailParserPathError instead of ValueError so the broader catch cannot swallow them.Deduplication was hardened in the same change: it reserves room for its own suffix marker(write_sample() sanitizes again, and the clamp there used to cut the marker back off,collapsing distinct attachments onto one file), resumes from the last used suffix per steminstead of rescanning from 1 (quadratic before — 16000 same-named attachments took 14 s, nowmilliseconds), and folds case, because APFS, exFAT and SMB collapse Invoice.pdf andinvoice.pdf.WorkaroundsUpgrade to 4.6.3. If you cannot upgrade, do not call write_attachments() on untrusted mail;iterate parser.attachments yourself and write each attachment inside its owntry/except Exception, skipping the ones whose safe_filename is None.Referenceshttps://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-8cgq-x343-p74chttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129301https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/pull/171https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/commit/11b894a0b8b3f11055a99caff118206138d1dabahttps://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/commit/e1d9fe6778045d6e2c44406bc8822e3464c1097fhttps://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/releases/tag/4.6.3https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8cgq-x343-p74c

items.title: [mail-parser] mail-parser: Uncaught `OverflowError` / `OSError` on an out-of-range `Received` date
items.summary:
ImpactA Received header whose trailing date carries an out-of-range year, or a timezone offsetlarge enough to push the timestamp past the int64 epoch range, raises an exception that isoutside the MailParser* hierarchy. A caller that catches only mail-parser exceptionsdoes not catch it, and the parse of the entire message is aborted — the same class of issueas GHSA-24mq-4vc6-2prf,which this survives (it is not a duplicate; 24mq is fixed in 4.6.2 and this reproduces on 4.6.2).All entry points are affected: parse_from_string(), parse_from_bytes(), parse_from_file(),parse_from_file_obj() and the mail-parser CLI. The header is fully attacker-controlled anda single line is enough, so any pipeline that parses untrusted mail can be made to lose themessage — and, if one worker handles a queue, to drop the batch.import mailparserraw = ("Received: from x ([1.2.3.4]) by mx.victim.com; "       "Tue, 7 Mar 292277026596 14:29:24 +0000

body
")mailparser.parse_from_string(raw).mail_json# <= 4.6.2 -> OverflowError: signed integer is greater than maximum# 4.6.3    -> parses; the unusable hop date is reported as "date_utc": nullRoot cause. receiveds_format() in src/mailparser/utils.py guarded the date conversionwith except (TypeError, ValueError), but convert_mail_date() → email.utils.mktime_tz() →calendar.timegm() raises OverflowError for years whose epoch seconds overflow int64, anddatetime.fromtimestamp() reports EOVERFLOW as OSError for a sufficiently large timezoneoffset. The date and timezone properties already wrapped the same conversion inexcept Exception; only the Received path was left open.Affected range. Introduced by the date-handling change in ca2aa6a, first released in3.7.0. Reproduced on PyPI 3.7.0, 3.8.0, 3.9.3, 4.0.0, 4.5.0, 4.6.0, 4.6.2 and on masterbefore the fix (Python 3.14). 3.6.0 is not affected.PatchesFixed in 4.6.3. receiveds_format() now also catches OverflowError and OSError andrecords date_utc = None for that hop, so the rest of the message still parses:try:    j["date_utc"], _ = convert_mail_date(i["date"])except (TypeError, ValueError, OverflowError, OSError):    j["date_utc"] = NoneA sweep of year magnitudes from 10^7 to 10^12 shows only ValueError, OverflowError andOSError are reachable on this path.WorkaroundsUpgrade to 4.6.3. If you cannot upgrade, wrap every parse_from_* call in a bareexcept Exception rather than except MailParserError, and treat the message as unparsed.ReferencesFix: https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/pull/171Related: GHSA-24mq-4vc6-2prfReferenceshttps://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-xhrq-2mqv-q8wxhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129300https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/pull/171https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/commit/d69f6f9b6ad0bf74d731b373bbdeabb462c32b26https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/commit/e1d9fe6778045d6e2c44406bc8822e3464c1097fhttps://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/releases/tag/4.6.3https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xhrq-2mqv-q8wx

items.title: [mail-parser] mail-parser: Uncaught exceptions and silent header loss in mail-parser on attacker-controlled input
[mail-parser] mail-parser: Sender IP address spoofing in get_server_ipaddress()
items.summary: PatchesFixed in 4.6.2. Upgrade with pip install --upgrade mail-parser.Candidate addresses are now selected by position, not by appearance — a bracketed addressthe sender wrote is byte-identical to one the MTA wrote, so no amount of pattern matchingcan tell them apart:the first token of the from clause is the HELO name, whatever its shape, and is never acandidate;an explicit HELO marker inside a comment group is sender text and is excluded;a candidate must sit inside a ( / [ group;IPv4 and IPv6 matches are merged positionally, never family-first;the walk stops at the first trusted hop naming no address, rather than continuing intosender-written headers.The IPv6 pattern was corrected to skip the IPv6: tag and to prefer the longest valid form.Behaviour change. get_server_ipaddress() now returns None rather than an unreliablevalue in two cases that previously returned an address: a from clause consisting of a bareaddress with no HELO marker (indistinguishable from EHLO <that address>), and a trusted hopnaming no address at all. Callers must handle None.WorkaroundsNone within mail-parser. Callers who cannot upgrade should not treat the return value ofget_server_ipaddress() as trustworthy, and should derive sender attribution from anauthenticated signal instead — the MTA's own logs, or SPF/DKIM/DMARC results computedoutside this library.Referenceshttps://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-72px-j8gh-p79xhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129297https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/pull/167https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/commit/ce3cf3559db1ff806bda598b378de9f8c2a5be96https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/releases/tag/4.6.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-72px-j8gh-p79x

items.title: [mail-parser] mail-parser is vulnerable to polynomial ReDoS in email header parsing
items.summary: SummaryTwo regular expressions used while parsing email headers backtrackpolynomially on attacker-controlled input. Parsing a single small, well-formedemail can consume minutes to hours of CPU, denying service to any process thatparses untrusted mail.Both are reachable from an ordinary parse_from_string(), parse_from_bytes()or parse_from_file() call — no special API, option, or malformed structure isrequired by the victim.Details1. Address-header fallback regex (src/mailparser/utils.py)get_addresses() falls back to _ADDR_FALLBACK_RE wheneveremail.utils.getaddresses(strict=True) yields no usable address. Thealternative ([^<,]*?)\s*<([^>]+)> overlaps a lazy quantifier with an adjacent\s* — a space matches both. Driven by finditer, which retries at everyoffset and rescans the remainder, matching degrades to quadratic on <padding and cubic on whitespace padding.The fallback engages on the feature's own happy path, e.g.From: alice@example.com <bob@example.com>.Measured (4.6.0, CPython 3.14, macOS arm64; reproduced identically on Linux andon CPython 3.9, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13):PaddingParse timevalid address + 750 sp0.38 s+ 1500 sp2.97 s+ 3000 sp23.4 s (×7.9/2×)+ 6 KB sp185 s~100 KB sphoursFully RFC 5322-compliant folded headers (all lines ≤ 71 octets) trigger the sameblowup, so the input passes normal MTA and library checks. ~100 KB of headers iswithin Postfix's default header_size_limit = 102400.All six address headers parsed by the library (From, To, Cc, Bcc,Reply-To, Delivered-To) are affected and their cost adds up linearly.2. Received-header clause splitter (src/mailparser/const.py)parse_received() splits on _CLAUSE_SPLITTER,(?:^|\s+)(from|by|via|with|id|for|envelope-from)\s+. Under re.split thisbacktracks quadratically over any whitespace run that is not followed by aclause keyword. The pre-existing normalization collapsed only [\t\n], soliteral spaces — including folded-header padding — reached the splitter intact.Measured: 24 000 spaces in one Received: header → 22 s; ~100 KB → minutes.ImpactAvailability. A handful of small emails keeps every parsing worker of a mailgateway, ticketing system, quarantine UI, or archiving pipeline permanentlybusy. No confidentiality or integrity impact.Anyone who parses email they did not author is affected — which is the library'spurpose.PatchesFixed in 4.6.1.The address fallback is now a linear scan: the header is split intocomma-separated items (quote-aware, in Python), then each item is matchedagainst a bounded angle-address <([^<>\s]+)> with the display name derivedin Python, falling back to a bare-email match. Each pattern has a singlenon-nested quantifier over a negated character class → O(n).2000 padding spaces: 3.5 s → <0.01 s. 256 KB padding: hours → 0.087 s.Output is preserved on every previously supported shape.parse_received() collapses whitespace runs to a single space beforesplitting, so the splitter's \s+ only ever matches one character → O(n).The date is extracted from the raw header beforehand, so date formatting isunaffected. 24 000 spaces: 22 s → 0.003 s; 200 000 spaces: 0.004 s.Regression tests assert linear-time behaviour for both paths.WorkaroundsNone within the library. Upgrade to 4.6.1.Users who cannot upgrade immediately should cap total header size beforeparsing and enforce a wall-clock timeout around each parse.Referenceshttps://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-r7w7-vpq8-c5vvhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129295https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/pull/166https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/commit/037293158cb291caa96635a54449243d32cd4d96https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/commit/5aab122f0d763991604d2c2bcc807c6bf2489464https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/commit/85e53f820d78ae7c955dafbbcd0e20989a735c2chttps://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/releases/tag/4.6.1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r7w7-vpq8-c5vv

items.title: [mail-parser] mail-parser: Path Traversal vulnerability in attachment extraction
items.summary: A path traversal vulnerability was identified in mail-parser when extracting email attachments using the write_attachments() and write_sample() APIs.A specially crafted email containing malicious attachment filenames (for example, using directory traversal sequences such as "../" or absolute filesystem paths) could cause files to be written outside the intended output directory. Depending on how the library was used and the permissions of the executing process, this could result in arbitrary file overwrite.The vulnerability affects mail-parser versions 3.8.0 through 4.5.0.The issue has been addressed by introducing comprehensive filename sanitization and path validation before any file is written to disk. The fix includes:Sanitization of attachment filenames before writing.Validation that all output paths remain within the intended destination directory.Rejection of symbolic link targets.Normalization of Windows and POSIX path separators.Validation and rejection of invalid or unsafe filenames.Protection applied consistently in both write_attachments() and write_sample() APIs.Users are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the patched release.CreditsThe vulnerability was responsibly reported by Niranjan Ganesan (Security Insights, https://securityinsights.io/, GitHub: @iam-niranjan).The vulnerability was analyzed, remediated, and the security fix was implemented by Fedele Mantuano, maintainer of mail-parser (LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/fmantuano/).mail-parser would like to thank Niranjan Ganesan for following a coordinated vulnerability disclosure process and for collaborating throughout the remediation and verification of the fix.Referenceshttps://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-fr3h-cpq2-9496https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129296https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/pull/165https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/commit/3d6cb7a51f2ad7ea57e529121dbd5d56f29fefe8https://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/commit/b0a2e968815f3ed9e129efb0f5f7e935a9dacd1dhttps://github.com/SpamScope/mail-parser/releases/tag/4.6.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fr3h-cpq2-9496

items.title: [termux-sync] termux-sync: Arbitrary file write during restore via attacker-controlled manifest source path
items.summary: termux-sync restore trusts fields inside an untrusted backup manifest and uses them as the extraction destination without validation.During restore, each archive entry is handled as:  src_dir = Path(info.get("source", ...)).parent  extract_archive(archive, src_dir, ...)extract_archive opens the archive and runs tarfile.extract for every member with no path jail and no filter:  with tarfile.open(archive_path, "r:*") as tf:      for member in tf.getmembers():          tf.extract(member, dest_path, set_attrs=True)There is no check that manifest "source" stays under an expected restore root, that tar members stay inside dest_path, or that backup_name used in temporary paths cannot contain ".." or separators.Impact:A victim who restores a malicious backup (local, shared, or from a compromised GitHub/Google Drive storage backend) can have arbitrary files written anywhere the Termux user can write. Overwriting shell startup files or executable scripts leads to local code execution on later use.Reproduction (benign markers only):Build a backup directory with home.tar.gz (members: proof filename + optional config names) and manifest.json.Set files.home.source to any path whose parent is the desired write directory (e.g. $HOME/dummy_for_parent so parent is $HOME).Run the same extract path the tool uses: src_dir = Path(source).parent; tarfile.extract each member into src_dir.Observe attacker-controlled files created under $HOME and under other chosen roots (config / shell-rc style overwrite).Expected: restore only writes under fixed, validated roots; reject unsafe source values and members that resolve outside dest.Actual: write destination is fully controlled by manifest.source; proof files and overwrites appear outside any intended jail.Fix direction:Do not trust manifest "source" for extract roots; use fixed app-defined destinationsSanitize backup_name (basename; reject ".." and separators)Extract with tarfile filter="data" (or equivalent boundary checks) and refuse escapeTreat backups as untrusted inputActual result (local marker-only reproduction):PROOF path: /data/data/com.termux/files/home/PWNED_BY_TERMUX_SYNC_RESTORE.txtPROOF exists? TruePROOF content:PWNEDThis file was written by a malicious termux-sync backup restore path.Root cause: manifest files.*.source controls extract destination.*** VULN CONFIRMED: arbitrary write to $HOME ***important.conf => secret=ATTACKER_CONTROLLED*** VULN CONFIRMED: overwrite under attacker-chosen root ***.bashrc_sim shows injected:export ATTACKER=1*** VULN CONFIRMED: startup-file style overwrite ***Extract roots used:  home  -> parent($HOME/dummy_for_parent) = $HOME  config -> parent(.../victim_sim/nested_dummy) = .../victim_simReported and credited to Niranj R Mahaswar ( GitHub: @NiranjMahaswar )Referenceshttps://github.com/djunekz/termux-sync/security/advisories/GHSA-259w-wmqg-fp76https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-86046https://github.com/djunekz/termux-sync/commit/9c8637b280ee3e126885def5ff5b326c289ee7cfhttps://github.com/djunekz/termux-sync/releases/tag/v1.2.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-259w-wmqg-fp76

items.title: [nltk] NLTK dot2img runs Graphviz 'dot' without the trusted-exec chokepoint, enabling local code execution via a writable PATH element
items.summary:
Summarynltk.parse.dependencygraph.dot2img invokes the Graphviz dot executable without the trusted-execution guarantees that NLTK applies to its other native-tool wrappers. The function resolves dot by bare name and then runs the resolved absolute path with a raw subprocess.run, omitting the ownership/writability check and the loader-environment scrub that nltk.pathsec.spawn_trusted provides. On a POSIX host, a local, unprivileged actor who can write to any group/world-writable directory that appears on the victim's PATH can plant a trojan dot; when the victim later renders a DependencyGraph (for example in a Jupyter notebook, which auto-invokes _repr_svg_) or calls dot2img directly, the planted binary executes as the victim. The advisory GHSA-6hwm-xvph-95vm (CVE-2026-78680) addressed the same untrusted-search-path class for the Graphviz dot invoker in nltk/translate/api.py, but dot2img received only part of that remediation and remains exploitable.Root CauseNLTK's native-tool security model layers four defenses (documented in nltk/EXTERNAL_TOOL_SECURITY.md): (1) find_binary refuses a current-working-directory-relative match; (2) resolve_trusted_executable verifies the resolved file is a regular file that no other unprivileged user can replace (private parent directories, owner is the user or root, no group/world write bit); (3) shell execution is refused; (4) safe_env scrubs loader and interpreter environment variables before exec. Layers 2, 3, and 4 are reached only through nltk.pathsec.spawn_trusted. dot2img calls find_binary("dot") (layer 1 only), then executes the result with subprocess.run([dot_binary, ...]) and no env= argument. Layer 1 rejects only non-absolute matches, so an absolute path returned by the which search stage survives even when the file lives in a writable directory. Because dot2img never calls spawn_trusted, the ownership check and environment scrub never run.nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:626   dot_binary = find_binary("dot")          # layer 1 onlynltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:631   subprocess.run([dot_binary, "-T%s" % t], ...)   # no trust check, no env=nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:638   subprocess.run([dot_binary, "-T%s" % t], ...)   # binary-format branch, same gapnltk/internals.py:1034              if searching_bare_name and not os.path.isabs(path): continue  # skips only relative matchesnltk/translate/api.py:145           process = spawn_trusted(dot_binary, [f"-T{output_format}"], ...)  # hardened siblingImpactPrerequisites: a POSIX host on which the attacker is a local, unprivileged user (or code) able to write to a group/world-writable directory that appears on the victim's PATH. This includes the commonly cited case of a Homebrew /usr/local/bin with drwxrwxr-x permissions, or a writable directory placed early on PATH. The attacker plants a trojan dot there. When the victim renders a DependencyGraph (notebook _repr_svg_ auto-invocation) or calls dot2img directly, the trojan executes as the victim, yielding arbitrary local code execution in the victim's account: a local privilege-escalation and lateral-movement primitive. Because the child environment is not scrubbed, loader-injection variables (for example LD_PRELOAD, DYLD_*, GCONV_PATH) also reach the child, providing an additional execution surface. No control over NLTK inputs is required.Proof of ConceptRequires: POSIX host, an importable NLTK build from the affected tree, and Python 3. No third-party dependencies.Create a world-writable directory and write an executable dot script into it that drops a marker and emits fake SVG.Prepend that directory to PATH and run from a neutral working directory (so this is not the current-working-directory vector).Show that resolve_trusted_executable refuses the planted binary (so the hardened path would raise) while dot2img executes it.import os, stat, tempfile, subprocess, sysd = tempfile.mkdtemp()dot = os.path.join(d, "dot")with open(dot, "w") as f:    f.write("#!/bin/sh
touch " + os.path.join(d, "MARKER") + "
echo '<svg><!-- planted dot ran --></svg>'
")os.chmod(dot, 0o777)os.chmod(d, 0o777)os.environ["PATH"] = d + os.pathsep + os.environ["PATH"]os.chdir("/")from nltk.pathsec import resolve_trusted_executablefrom nltk.parse.dependencygraph import dot2imgprint("resolve_trusted_executable(planted dot):", resolve_trusted_executable(os.path.join(d, "dot")))out = dot2img("digraph G { a -> b }")print("dot2img stdout:", repr(out))print("planted dot executed (marker created):", os.path.exists(os.path.join(d, "MARKER")))resolve_trusted_executable(planted dot): Nonedot2img stdout: '<svg><!-- planted dot ran --></svg>
'planted dot executed (marker created): TrueAttack ChainExposure: On a shared POSIX host, a group/world-writable directory is present on the victim's PATH (for example a writable directory early on PATH, or a Homebrew /usr/local/bin with group-write). The attacker writes a trojan dot into it.Control: The attacker fully controls the contents of the planted dot file; no contro

items.title: [aiohttp] AIOHTTP: Event loop stall in add_domain() wildcard matching
items.summary: SummaryApplication.add_domain() compiled each * in a host mask to [^:]*. With two or more wildcards in a mask, matching a long Host header that does not match the mask took polynomial time on the event loop.ImpactAn attacker could stall a server that registers a domain mask with more than one wildcard by sending requests with a long Host header.WorkaroundUse at most one * in a domain mask.Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/c6ac0e44c3c573ff9616f4a6a532992538b31e43Referenceshttps://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/security/advisories/GHSA-jm3w-gw2p-xjfjhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-128124https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/pull/13943https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/pull/13945https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/766b882820da0651c84090e366a3b024b4a263c9https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/c6ac0e44c3c573ff9616f4a6a532992538b31e43https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/releases/tag/v3.14.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jm3w-gw2p-xjfj

items.title: [aiohttp] AIOHTTP: Unbounded cookie storage in client CookieJar
items.summary: SummarySet-Cookie parsing created additional cookies from unrecognised name=value attributes, and CookieJar had no limit on the number of cookies stored or sent. A server could make the client store a very large number of cookies and generate very large Cookie headers.ImpactA malicious server could cause excessive memory and CPU use in a client, repeated on every redirect, and cause later requests to the same domain to build an excessively large Cookie header.Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/6963ee0befec1502b6bb7b4db6c72d044c08f4faReferenceshttps://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/security/advisories/GHSA-5pv8-vvhc-h7jvhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-128125https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/pull/13930https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/pull/13942https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/6963ee0befec1502b6bb7b4db6c72d044c08f4fahttps://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/b1f6c87b2bd3bd80f2b6c22ff46e11d00921e412https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/releases/tag/v3.14.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5pv8-vvhc-h7jv

items.title: [aiohttp] AIOHTTP: Too many URL-encoded form fields block the event loop
items.summary: SummaryRequest.post() had no limit on the number of fields in a URL-encoded form body. Inserting a large number of repeated keys into a MultiDict took quadratic time on the event loop.ImpactAn attacker could block the event loop with a form POST within the default client_max_size to any handler that calls Request.post().Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/615fec3d4f088f30d2ee72cad760152e92aa1c53Referenceshttps://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/security/advisories/GHSA-xgw8-8ccx-rmqhhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-128126https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/pull/13738https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/pull/13741https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/615fec3d4f088f30d2ee72cad760152e92aa1c53https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/8b0100572936df28977b9de8a6cc7e464c0b521ehttps://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/releases/tag/v3.14.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xgw8-8ccx-rmqh

items.title: [aiohttp] AIOHTTP: Base64 multipart parts bypass client_max_size
items.summary: SummaryWhen reading a multipart part with Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64, BodyPartReader.read_chunk() kept reading until the chunk length was a multiple of 4, with no byte limit. A part with a short Content-Length, or a long run of whitespace, could cause the entire remaining body to be read into memory within a single call before any size check, or spin on the event loop.ImpactAn attacker could bypass client_max_size to cause excessive memory use, or block the event loop, with a specially crafted multipart request to any handler that reads multipart data.Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/a555ab698e08e9baea7386d5b4c0761cb8956fddReferenceshttps://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/security/advisories/GHSA-24c4-3p7v-29cmhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-128127https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/pull/13509https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/pull/13513https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/2d9c5c1062eff0034fb3ab120897a6c1b3ff7041https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/a555ab698e08e9baea7386d5b4c0761cb8956fddhttps://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/releases/tag/v3.14.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-24c4-3p7v-29cm
